segments.text: The question was simple. Could this SHA-3 implementation be improved?
Here's what changed and what the measurements show.
Start with Oxide's Quartz Core. One byte arrives each clock.
Two block buffers let it fill the next block while processing the previous one.
That's a good match for its byte stream workload.
With the full-rate adapter, this integration reaches nearly 100 megabytes per second.

chapters.title: Compact: absorb directly into the state

segments.text: Now look at the wider path. DMA already delivers eight bytes at a time. A small buffer feeds those
bytes straight into the hash state. Both full block buffers disappear. The digest reads the state
itself. Capture and absorption still take separate cycles and the permutation still takes 24 rounds.
The next step was simplifying the surrounding logic.
Padding only touches 17 lanes, so the selector doesn't need to reach across all 25.
Framing errors are also registered before updating the state.
The compact version keeps the same simulated cycle count, with fewer stand-alone lookup tables.
Now look at the resource counts. About 23% fewer lookup tables, 58% fewer flip-flops.
Those totals include the local adapters, so the comparison covers the complete routed hash partitions.
Both use zero block RAM and zero DSP blocks.
Both cores use the same board, shell, driver, and 100 MHz clock.
The comparison uses the median of 7 samples after warm-up, with every digest checked against software.
Upload and reconfiguration are outside these timers.
Watch the time for a 16 MB message.
Quartz takes about 169 milliseconds.
Compact takes 72.
That's 2.36 times the DMA throughput.
Through the Processing System API,
the gain is 1.91 times,
with copying and request overheads still included.
Quartz still wins the small requests in these measurements.
This improvement applies to large buffers on this board.
The reserved region and image size are unchanged.
Power and oxide production system performance weren't measured.
